text: You're in the situation I've been in for the last couple of years competing, the permanent "gaintainer." Whether this is a good thing or not, experts still debate. Some debate there's "No way you can build strength while staying the same weight!", or rather you can, but eventually it tapers off... And there's plenty of experts and coaches that say the opposite. I've hovered at 226-228 for nearly two years now, and all of my competition performances have continued to go up... So I can say it works for me. Maybe it will for you. As for the next eight weeks, remember that a couple of kilos is not something you really have to "CUT" cut for. If I'm eating for performance and, like, a week out I notice I'm super-close to 231, I'll just spend a few days of deload week eating low carb, drink a whole bunch of a water in the first half of the week, a lot, and by Thursday or Friday I'll be like 225-226. 5 lbs is literally just sodium and water weight, so unless you eat fast food on a regular basis, it shouldn't be hard to drop a bit heading into the meet. If it were me, I'd stick with the lower weight class because you're basically there right now. It's either that or start heading toward the higher weight class, and set yourself up for a water cut.

text: This is an interesting routine that strikes a balance between muscular hypertrophy and cardio vascular conditioning. It excels in that is hits every major muscle group several times a week, in programming a full body work out each session, and through targeting calorically intense motions. It is limited in that it prioritizes exercise over training. This is to say that it would be challenging to progress on some of these lifts in controlled ways. Further, there is an implied artificial distinction between weight loss and muscle growth. In reality, bigger muscles require more energy to maintain. Technically, this may cause you to weigh more (famously muscle is heavier than fat). However, a lb of muscle requires more calories to maintain than a lb of fat. would it be better to do 3 sets? This depends. If you're enjoying yourself, then proceed accordingly. For me, I would at minimum start each session with the leg lifts since legs contain the most muscle and therefore consume the most oxygen. This is a good foundation and you will progress towards your goals if you continue to train regularly, increase either the weight or volume at controlled intervals, replenish your body with nutritious food, and get good sleep. Consider re-evaluating if this stops bringing joy, or if you are unable to increase the volume or weight of your lifts at regular intervals
label: advice_analysis
